en: Mahāniddesa, Aṭṭhakavagga, 10. Purābhedasuttaniddesa:
Exposition of the Discourse on the Prior Breach.
Now he will explain the exposition of the "Discourse on the Breach of the City":
"How should one see, how should one conduct oneself,
to be called 'peaceful'?"
Tell me that, O Gotama, when asked, you supreme man: How does one see,
how does one conduct oneself, so as to be called "peaceful"?
"How does he see? means: endowed with what kind of seeing? Of what shape? Of what sort? Of what appearance?—thus, "how does he see?
"How is his virtue? means: endowed with what kind of virtue? Of what shape? Of what sort? Of what appearance?—thus, "how is his virtue?"

"How is he in view? How is he in virtue? Why is he called 'calmed'? One who is "peaceful" (santo) is said, proclaimed, spoken of, declared, illustrated, and designated as "calmed," "thoroughly calmed," "fully calmed," "extinguished," and "tranquilized.
"How is he in view? asks concerning higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*). "How is he in virtue? asks concerning higher morality (*adhisīla*). "Calmed" asks concerning higher mind (*adhicitta*).
"How should one see, how should one conduct oneself, to be called 'peaceful'? Tell me that, Gotama.
"That" refers to what I ask, what I entreat, what I beseech, and what I inspire with confidence.
"Gotama"—thus that created being addressed the Blessed Buddha by his clan name.
"Speak forth"—that is: speak, declare, teach, make known, establish, set forth, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain.
"Tell that to me, Gotama."
"Asked, 'O supreme among men'":
"Asked" means questioned, asked, entreated, requested, or propitiated.
"Supreme among men" means the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the preeminent, the highest, and the most excellent among men.
Being questioned, he spoke to that supreme man:
“Of what appearance and of what conduct is he? Thus spoke that created being.
"One is called 'peaceful'—
tell me that, O Gotama,
supreme among men, when you are asked."
"Free from craving before his dissolution,
O Blessed One,
not dependent on the past," so it was said.
He is not to be reckoned as being in the middle;
for him there is nothing placed before him.
Free from craving before his passing away.

Before the breaking up of the body, before the breaking up of the selfhood, before the casting off of the corpse, and before the cutting off of the life-faculty—[he is] free from craving, devoid of craving, abandoned of craving, vomited out of craving, released from craving, relinquished of craving, renounced of craving;
free from passion, devoid of passion, abandoned of passion, vomited out of passion, released from passion, relinquished of passion, renounced of passion; he is without hunger.
Extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, he dwells having become Brahmā himself.
“Bhagavā” is a designation for one who possesses reverence;
moreover, he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed passion (*bhagga-rāgo*).
The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed hatred;
the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed delusion;
the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed pride.
The Blessed One has destroyed wrong views;
the Blessed One has destroyed craving;
the Blessed One has destroyed the defilements.
The Blessed One has enjoyed, distributed, and shared the jewel of the Dhamma;
the Blessed One brings an end to states of existence;
the Blessed One is one whose body is cultivated, whose virtue is cultivated, whose mind is cultivated, and whose wisdom is cultivated.
The Blessed One frequented remote lodgings in forest groves and jungle thickets—places with little sound, little noise, secluded from people, hidden away from men, and suitable for retreat;
thus he is the Blessed One. Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal herbs as support for the sick; thus he is the Blessed One.
Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, the flavor of liberation, of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom; thus he is the Blessed One.
Or else, the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive dwellings in attainment;
or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the ten developments of wisdom, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainments of the foul.

The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;

or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha.
"Bhagavā" is not a name given by a mother, nor by a father, nor by a brother,
nor by a sister, nor by friends and colleagues, nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities; rather,
this is a designation realized at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, simultaneously with the attainment of omniscient knowledge— namely, "Bhagavā."
"One whose craving has been removed before the breaking up [of the body]," said the Blessed One.
"Independent of the past" means that the past is called the prior limit (*pubbantamanta*).
Craving directed toward the past time has been abandoned, and views have been relinquished because craving has been abandoned and views have been relinquished.
In this way too, one does not rely on the past.
Or else, one does not take delight therein, thinking, "I was such-and-such in form in the past," or "I was such-and-such in feeling..."
‘I had such perception...
such volitional formations...
such consciousness in the past,’ one does not take delight therein.
Thus too, one does not rely on the past.

Or alternatively, regarding the thought, "Such was my eye in the past, such were the forms," consciousness is not bound by desire and lust therein; because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in that.
Not delighting in that.
Thus, too, one does not rely on the past:
"In this way my hearing was in the past time—"
“Such were sounds,” “In this way my nose was in the past—
such were odors,” “In this way my tongue was in the past—
such were flavors,” “In this way my body was in the past— ”

"Thus were tangibles," "thus was my mind in the past," or "thus were mental phenomena"—in these cases, consciousness is not bound by desire and lust. Because consciousness is not bound by desire and lust, one does not delight in them;
not delighting in them, [one does not cling].
In this way too, he does not depend on the past.

Or else, those things which were formerly laughed at, talked over, and played with by him together with women—he does not relish them, he does not desire them, and he does not find satisfaction in them.
In this way too, he does not depend on the past.
"In the middle, it is not to be reckoned":
"Middle" refers to the present time.
With reference to the present time, craving has been abandoned and views have been relinquished.
Because craving has been abandoned and views have been relinquished,

he is not to be described as "lustful," not to be described as "hated," not to be described as "deluded," not to be described as "bound," not to be described as "misapprehending," not to be described as "wavering," not to be described as "gone to what is undesirable," and not to be described as "deeply rooted."
Those volitional formations have been abandoned;

because volitional formations have been abandoned, he cannot be reckoned by way of destination—as one bound for hell, or one born in the animal realm, or one in the sphere of hungry ghosts, or a human, or a deva;
nor as one possessing form, or formless, or percipient, or non-percipient.
Or “neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
There is no cause, no condition, no reason by which it could be so designated;
thus, it is not to be designated as being in the middle.
"For him there is no honoring.
"For him" means for the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Honoring" refers to two kinds of honoring:
There is that which has craving as its primary focus and that which has views as its primary focus ... [as before] ...
this is that which has craving as its primary focus ... [as before] ... this is that which has views as its primary focus.
For him, the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished.

Because the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished, he does not walk about placing either craving or views before him; he has no banner of craving, no standard of craving, and is not dominated by craving, nor does he have a banner of views.
He does not have views as his banner, nor is he dominated by views; he does not wander surrounded by craving or views.
In this way, too, there is nothing held in front of him.
Or else, he does not bring about delight in the thought, "May I be of such a form in the future."
“May I have such feeling… may I have such perception… may I have such volitional formations….”
‘May I have such a consciousness in the future’—he does not take delight therein.
Thus, he has no preconceived preference.
Or again: ‘May my eye be thus in the future’—
Thinking, "Such forms," he does not direct his mind toward the acquisition of what has not yet been acquired. Because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in them;
not delighting in them, even in this way, there is nothing cherished by him.
“Thus may my ear exist in the future time—thus sounds”;
“Thus may my nose exist in the future time—thus odors”;
“Thus may my tongue exist in the future time—”
Thus, regarding tastes, thus regarding the body in the future,
thus regarding tangibles, and thus regarding the mind in the future, thus regarding mental objects—
he does not direct his mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained; because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in them.
Not delighting in that, even so there is nothing for him to hold before him.
Or else: "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a deva."
Or, thinking “another god,” he does not direct his mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained; because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in it;
not delighting in it, thus too there is nothing held as foremost by him.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Free from craving before his dissolution...
(Thus said the Blessed One).
Not dependent on what is before,
not to be reckoned by what is in the middle,
for him there is nothing placed ahead.
Free from anger, without fear,
not boastful, and without hypocrisy;
speaking with wisdom and free from agitation.
"He is indeed a sage restrained in speech, free from anger and without fear. Regarding the phrase "free from anger":
it is said that he is one who has abandoned anger.
Furthermore, anger should first be discussed.
Anger arises in ten ways:
anger arises [with the thought], "He has done me harm."
“Anger arises because ‘he has done me harm’;
anger arises because ‘he will do me harm’; anger arises because ‘he has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me’...”
Anger arises [when one thinks]: "He has acted for my harm...
he will act for my harm," or "He has acted for the benefit of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me..."
Anger arises when one thinks, "He has acted for my benefit… he will act for my benefit," or anger arises in an inappropriate situation.
Whatever such resentment, hostility, antipathy, and opposition of the mind; anger, rage, and fury; malice, spite, and surliness;
corruption of the mind and mental corruption; wrath, being angry, and the state of being angry; hatred, hating, and the state of hating;
malevolence, being malevolent, and the state of being malevolent; opposition and antagonism—this is called ill will.
Harshness, irritability, and mental dissatisfaction—
this is called anger. Furthermore,
the relative intensity of anger, whether excessive or slight, should be understood.
At times, anger is merely a state of mental agitation, yet it does not yet manifest as a contortion of the face;
at times, anger is merely a contortion of the face, yet it does not yet manifest as a clenching of the jaw;
at times, anger is merely a clenching of the jaw, yet it does not yet manifest as the utterance of harsh speech.
At some times anger consists merely in the utterance of harsh speech, but it does not yet involve looking about in all directions;
at some times anger consists merely in looking about in all directions, but it does not yet involve the grasping of sticks and weapons;
at some times anger consists merely in the grasping of sticks and weapons, but it does not yet involve the hurling of sticks and weapons.
At times, anger consists merely in the brandishing of sticks and weapons, yet it does not yet involve the striking with sticks and weapons;
at times, anger consists merely in the striking with sticks and weapons, yet it does not yet involve the maiming and mutilating;
at times, anger consists merely in the maiming and mutilating, yet it does not yet involve the breaking and crushing.
At times anger is merely a breaking and crushing, yet it does not yet involve the wrenching of limb from limb;
at times anger is merely the wrenching of limb from limb, yet it does not yet involve the taking of life;
at times anger is merely the taking of life, yet it does not yet reach the point of total renunciation and relinquishment.
Since anger destroys another person and thereby destroys oneself, it is at this point that anger has reached its highest peak and attained its greatest expansion.
One for whom that anger is abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, subsided, incapable of arising again, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge, is called "one without anger.
He is "without anger" because anger has been abandoned; he is "without anger" because the basis for anger has been fully understood; he is "without anger" because the cause of anger has been severed.
"Free from anger.
"Without trepidation" means that here someone is timid, easily startled, and apprehensive; he trembles, is startled, is apprehensive, fears, and falls into a state of terror, thinking:
"I do not obtain a family, or I do not obtain a group, or I do not obtain a dwelling, or I do not obtain gain."
If one does not obtain fame, or does not obtain praise, or does not obtain happiness,
or does not obtain robes, or does not obtain almsfood, or does not obtain lodgings, or does not obtain medicinal requisites for the sick,
or does not obtain an attendant for the sick, one trembles, fears, and is terrified, thinking, "I am lacking in wisdom."
He fears and falls into terror.
Here, a bhikkhu is not fearful, not terrified, and not apprehensive;
he does not tremble, does not fear, does not become apprehensive, and does not fall into terror.
I do not obtain a family, or I do not obtain a group, or I do not obtain a residence, or I do not obtain gain, or I do not obtain fame,
or I do not obtain praise, or I do not obtain happiness, or I do not obtain robes, or I do not obtain almsfood,
or I do not obtain lodgings, or I do not obtain medicinal requisites for the sick.
Or, if he does not obtain almsfood, or does not obtain an attendant for when he is ill, thinking "I am unknown," he does not tremble,
does not fear, does not shrink back, does not become afraid, and does not fall into terror;
thus he is "free from anger and free from fear."
"Not boastful, not devious.
Here, someone is a boaster, a pretender; he boasts and pretends, thinking:
"I am endowed with virtue," or "I am endowed with observances," or "I am endowed with both virtue and observances."
Whether by birth, or clan, or lineage, or beauty of complexion, or wealth, or Vedic study, or field of occupation,
or field of craft, or branch of science, or learning, or eloquence, or by some other such basis:

"He has gone forth from a high family," or "he has gone forth from a great family," or "he has gone forth from a family of great wealth," or "he has gone forth from a family of magnificent wealth," or "he is well-known and famous among householders and renunciants."
Or [thinking]: "I am one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick"; or "I am a master of the Suttas," or "a bearer of the Vinaya," or "an expounder of the Dhamma";
or "a forest-dweller," or "an alms-food eater," or "a wearer of rag-robes," or "one who possesses only three robes";
or "one who goes on a continuous round for alms," or "one who eats only from the bowl once," or "one who remains in a sitting posture," or "one who accepts whatever seat is offered."
Whether as one who has attained the first jhāna, or as one who has attained the second jhāna, or as one who has attained the third jhāna, or as one who has attained the fourth jhāna;
or as one who has attained the sphere of infinite space,
or the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness.
He does not boast or vaunt himself, thinking, "I am an attainer of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus he does not boast or vaunt himself; being free from boasting and vaunting, detached, abstinent, fully abstinent, emerged, escaped, and liberated, he dwells with a mind for which no boundary can be set—thus he is one who does not boast.
"Free from remorse" (*akukkucca*): "Remorse" (*kukkucca*) refers to remorse regarding the hands, remorse regarding the feet, and remorse regarding both hands and feet;

it also refers to perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, perceiving what is allowable as unallowable, and perceiving what is improper time as proper time, or [perceiving] proper time [as improper].
Perception of the improper as proper, and perception of the proper as improper;
whatever such remorse, state of being remorseful, state of having been remorseful, mental regret, or mental anguish there is—
this is called remorse (*kukkucca*).
Moreover, remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise for two reasons: from what has been done and from what has not been done.
How do remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise from what has been done and what has not been done?
"I have committed a bodily misconduct, I have failed to perform a bodily good deed"—thus does remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise.
“‘I have committed verbal misconduct; I have failed to practice verbal good conduct… I have committed mental misconduct;
I have failed to practice mental good conduct’”—thus there arises remorse, a state of mental regret, and a sense of mental anguish.
“I have committed the taking of life; I have not practiced abstention from the taking of life”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
“I have committed the taking of what is not given; I have not practiced abstention from the taking of what is not given”—thus [arises remorse].
Remorse arises, mental regret, and mental anguish:
"I have committed sexual misconduct; I have failed to abstain from sexual misconduct"—thus remorse arises, mental regret, and mental anguish.
“I have committed false speech; I have not practiced abstention from false speech.
… “I have committed malicious speech; I have not practiced abstention from malicious speech.
… “I have committed harsh speech; I have not practiced abstention from harsh speech. …
“Idle chatter has been committed by me; abstention from idle chatter has not been practiced by me”;
“… covetousness has been committed by me; non-covetousness has not been practiced by me”;
“… ill will has been committed by me; non-ill will has not been practiced by me.”
“Wrong view has been done by me; right view has not been done by me”—thus there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
In this way, through what has been done and what has not been done, there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
Or else, thinking, “I have not been one who fulfills my moral virtues,” there arises remorse, mental regret,
and inner distress; [thinking], “I have not guarded the doors of my sense faculties,”...
“I am one who lacks moderation in eating,” … “I am not devoted to wakefulness,” … “I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension,” …
“I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness,” … “I have not developed the four right efforts,” … “I have not developed the four bases for psychic power,” …
“‘The five faculties have not been developed by me’ … ‘The five powers have not been developed by me’ … ‘The seven factors of awakening have not been developed by me’ …”
“I have not cultivated the noble eightfold path,” … “suffering has not been fully understood by me,” … “the origin has not been abandoned by me,” …
“The path has not been developed by me”—
thus there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish. “Cessation has not been realized by me”— thus there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
One for whom this remorse has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one without remorse.
Thus he is "one who does not boast, one without remorse;
one who speaks with deliberation, one who is not agitated."
"Mantra" is said to be wisdom (*paññā*).
That which is wisdom, understanding... [as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
Having repeatedly grasped with such mantra, one speaks words—even when speaking much, reciting much, illuminating much, or communicating much.
He does not utter speech that is ill-spoken, ill-said, ill-proclaimed, ill-uttered, or ill-articulated;
thus he is one who speaks with deliberation. He is undisturbed.
In this context, what is restlessness?
That which is restlessness of mind, lack of tranquility, agitation of the mind, and unsteadiness of the mind—
this is called restlessness.
One for whom this restlessness has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "undisturbed. Thus:
"The sage who speaks with deliberation is undisturbed;
he is indeed one restrained in speech."
Here, a bhikkhu, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to the truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these [people] from those, nor having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those [people] from these.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, finds joy in concord, and speaks words that create concord.
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech;
he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-stirring, urbane, agreeable to many people, and beloved by many people. He speaks such words as these.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter;

he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he is one who utters speech that is worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, well-defined, and connected with the goal.
Endowed with these four forms of verbal good conduct, he speaks speech free from the four faults, and [abstains] from the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk.
He is detached, abstinent, refrained from [unwholesome things], emerged, escaped, liberated, and dissociated; he dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
He spoke on ten topics of discourse, namely:
he spoke on the discourse of fewness of desires, he spoke on the discourse of contentment, he spoke on the discourse of seclusion...
a talk on non-association … a talk on the arousal of energy … a talk on virtue …
a discourse on concentration … a discourse on wisdom … a discourse on liberation …
a discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation … a discourse on the foundations of mindfulness … a discourse on the right strivings …
the discourse on the bases of psychic power … the discourse on the faculties … the discourse on the powers …
a discourse on the factors of enlightenment … a discourse on the path … a discourse on the fruit …
He speaks on the discourse of Nibbāna.
"Vācāyato" means restrained, disciplined, guarded, protected, shielded, and stilled. A "muni" is one such as this.
"Mona" is said to be knowledge.
That which is wisdom, understanding... [as above] ...non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view...
[as above] ...having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (muni).
He is indeed a sage restrained in speech.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Free from anger, free from fear..."
One who does not boast, who is free from remorse,
who speaks with deliberation, and who is not agitated—
he indeed is a sage restrained in speech.
Free from attachment to the future,
he does not grieve for the past;
seeing solitude amidst sense contacts, he dwells with a mind well-restrained.
And one is not led away by views.
"Without attachment, not coming"—
attachment is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ...

covetousness, greed, and root of unwholesomeness there may be—when this attachment and craving have been abandoned by one, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus too is there non-attachment toward the future.
Or alternatively, one does not bring about delight therein by thinking, "May I be of such a form in the future," or "May I have such a feeling...
may I have such a perception..."
‘May I have such volitional formations in the future… may I have such consciousness in the future,’ one does not take delight therein.
Thus there is no attachment to the future.

Or else, he does not direct his mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained, thinking, "May my eye be thus in the future—may forms be thus"; because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in it;
not delighting in it, [he does not grasp at it].
In this way, too, there is no attachment regarding the future:
“Thus may my ear exist in the future time, and thus sounds. …pe…

Thinking, "May such be my mind in the future—may such be my states," he does not direct his heart toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained. Because of this lack of mental aspiration, he does not delight in that;
not delighting in it, [he does not grasp it].
Thus there is no attachment regarding the future.

Alternatively, one does not direct the mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained, thinking, "By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a god or some other kind of deity.
Because of this lack of mental aspiration, one does not delight in that.
Not rejoicing in that,
thus there is no attachment to the future;
one does not grieve for the past.
He does not grieve over an object that has changed, nor does he grieve when an object has changed; he does not grieve thinking, "My eye has changed," nor does he grieve thinking, "My ear...
my nose... has changed.
My tongue...
my body...
my forms...
Sounds are mine… scents are mine… tastes are mine…
Tangible objects are mine… my family is mine… my group is mine…
My dwelling...
my gain...
my fame...
Praise for me… happiness for me… a robe for me…
Almsfood is mine… lodging is mine… medicinal requisites for the sick are mine…
My mother...
my father...
my brother...
My sister...
my son...
my daughter...
They are my friends...
they are my ministers...
they are my kinsmen...
Thinking, "My kinsmen have passed away," he does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion;
thus, he does not sorrow for the past.
He is one who sees seclusion in sense contacts.
Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-contact;
contact through designation, contact through resistance; contact to be felt as pleasant, contact to be felt as painful, contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
wholesome contact, unwholesome contact, indeterminate contact; that which belongs to the sense-sphere.
Contact pertaining to the realm of form, contact pertaining to the formless realm; empty contact, signless contact, wishless contact;
worldly contact, supramundane contact; past contact, future contact, present contact;
whatever kind of contact there is—contacting, contacting thoroughly, the state of having contacted.
This is called contact.
"One who sees seclusion in contacts":
one sees eye-contact as secluded from a self or from what belongs to a self, as permanent, stable, eternal, or subject to no change.
He sees ear-contact as secluded...
he sees nose-contact as secluded...
he sees tongue-contact as secluded...
He sees body-contact as secluded… he sees mind-contact as secluded… he sees designation-contact as secluded…
He sees contact associated with aversion as secluded...
contact conducive to pleasant feeling...
contact conducive to painful feeling...
contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant … wholesome contact … unwholesome contact …
indeterminate contact … sense-sphere contact … fine-material-sphere contact …
He sees formless-sphere contact...
mundane contact as secluded from a self or from what belongs to a self, or as impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and subject to change.
Or else, he sees past contact as secluded from future and present contacts; [he sees] future [contact...]
He sees contact as secluded from past and present contacts; he sees present contact as secluded from past and future contacts.
Or alternatively, those contacts which are noble, taintless, supramundane, and associated with emptiness—in those contacts he sees seclusion.
One sees it as secluded from lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, contempt, domineering, envy, avarice,
deceit, fraud, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence, from all defilements,
all misconduct, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations— one sees it as secluded from these.
One who sees with discernment regarding contacts is not led away by views.
For him, the sixty-two types of speculative views have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, and calmed; they are incapable of arising again, having been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Thus, one is not led away by views, not carried off, not swept away, and not drawn along;
nor does one regard that course of views as essential, nor does one return to it— thus,
one is not led away among views.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Without attachment to the future,
he does not grieve for the past;”
One who sees with discernment is not led astray by sense contacts or by views; being withdrawn and free from guile,
he does not deceive.
Free from envy and without stinginess;
modest, free from impurity,
and not addicted to slander.
“Withdrawn and free from deceit. “Drawn back” means:

drawn back because of the abandoning of lust; drawn back because of the abandoning of hatred; drawn back because of the abandoning of delusion; drawn back because of the abandoning of anger … resentment … contempt … insolence … envy … avarice … [and so on] … drawn back because of the abandoning of all unwholesome volitional formations.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu withdrawn?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the conceit ‘I am,’ cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising.”
“In this way, monks, a monk is withdrawn”—thus he is withdrawn.
“Not fraudulent”:
there are three bases for fraud.
The basis for hypocrisy consists of the seeking of requisites, the deportment, and indirect hinting.
What is the basis for hypocrisy consisting of the seeking of requisites?
Here, householders invite a bhikkhu with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thus, one who is evil-desirous, overcome by desire, and seeking more— driven by a longing for further gain regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—
renounces robes, renounces almsfood, renounces lodgings,
and renounces medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thus he spoke:
"What need has a recluse for expensive robes?
It is fitting that a recluse should gather scraps from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, and having made them into a patched cloak, wear it."
"What need has the ascetic for costly almsfood?
It is fitting that the ascetic should maintain his life by means of the gleanings of food obtained through the practice of begging.
What need has the ascetic for costly lodgings?"
"It is fitting for a recluse to be one who dwells at the foot of trees, or in a charnel ground, or in the open air.
What need has a recluse for costly medicinal requisites for the sick?
It is fitting for a recluse to prepare medicine from fermented urine or pieces of myrobalan."
Relying on that, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse almsfood, uses a coarse resting place, and uses coarse medicinal requisites as support for the sick.
Householders perceive him thus:

“This ascetic is one of few desires, content, secluded, unattached, energetic, and a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhuta). They increasingly invite him with robes, almsfood, resting places, and medicinal requisites as support for the sick.
Thus he spoke:
“When three things are present, a clansman endowed with faith generates much merit.
Through the presence of faith, a clansman endowed with faith generates much merit; through the presence of the object to be given...”
A faithful clansman generates much merit; because of the presence of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman generates much merit:
"You have this faith, the gift to be given exists, and I am the recipient."
“If I do not accept it, you will thus be excluded from merit.
I have no need for this;
nevertheless, out of compassion for you alone, I accept it.”
On that basis, he accepts much robe-cloth, accepts much almsfood, accepts much lodging, and accepts much medicinal requisites for the sick.
Whatever such frowning, frownishness, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer there may be—
this is the ground for scheming known as the acceptance of requisites.
What is the basis for hypocrisy consisting of deportment?
Here, a certain person who is of evil desire, overcome by desire, and intent on gaining esteem— thinking, "In this way people will esteem me"—
composes his walking, composes his standing, composes his sitting, and composes his reclining, having made a resolve.
He goes with a fixed intention, stands with a fixed intention, sits with a fixed intention, and lies down with a fixed intention;
he goes as if concentrated, stands as if concentrated, sits as if concentrated, and lies down as if concentrated;
he is like one who meditates on what is within range of sight.
Whatever such assuming, placing, adjusting, contortion, contorting, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of scheming regarding one’s deportment— this is the ground for scheming known as deportment.
What is the ground for scheming known as indirect talk?
In this case, someone with evil desires, driven by craving and seeking esteem, speaks words based on the noble Dhamma, thinking,
"In this way people will hold me in high esteem. He says, "The ascetic who wears such a robe is one of great influence," or,
"He who wears such a bowl..."
He carries an iron bowl;
he carries a water-strainer;
he carries a water-scooper.
He carries a key;
he wears sandals;
he wears a waistband.
“He is a monk of great influence who maintains his application,” he says;
“He is a monk of great influence who has such a preceptor,” he says;
“He is a monk of great influence who has such a teacher…”
Such are those who have the same preceptor… those who have the same teacher… friends…
"He is seen face-to-face...
he is a fellow monk...
he is a companion; that ascetic is of great influence," he says.
“He who dwells in such a dwelling is a monk of great influence,” he says;
“he who dwells in such a half-joined house… dwells in a palace…”
He dwells in a hut… he dwells in a cave… he dwells in a rock shelter…
He dwells in a hut… he dwells in a gabled house… he dwells in a watchtower…
He dwells on the upper floor;
he dwells on the roof-terrace;
he dwells in the assembly hall.
“He dwells in a pavilion… he dwells at the foot of a tree; that ascetic is of great influence,” he says.
Or else, he is one who is excessively anxious, excessively frowning, deceitful, prone to deception, talkative, and flattering with his mouth.
Thinking, “This ascetic is one who has attained such peaceful abidings and meditative attainments,” he delivered a discourse that was profound,
hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness. Such grimacing, grimacery, scheming,
scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer— this is [dishonesty].
This is the ground for hypocrisy known as hinting.

One for whom these three grounds for hypocrisy have been abandoned, eradicated, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge— he is called "one who is not hypocritical"— that is,
one who is withdrawn and free from hypocrisy.
"Free from envy and not stingy.
Envy is called craving (*taṇhā*).
It is that which is lust, infatuation … [as above] … covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.

One for whom this longing—that thirst which has been abandoned, utterly destroyed, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—is called one who is free from longing.
He does not long for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles;
nor for a clan, a group, a dwelling, gain, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick.

… the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm … the immaterial realm … existence in the sense sphere … existence in the fine-material sphere … existence in the immaterial sphere … existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence … the past … the future … the present … and in the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
“He does not long for, desire, approve of, yearn for, or crave the Dhamma”— thus he is one who is without longing (*apihālu*).
“Not stingy” refers to the five kinds of stinginess:
Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Whatever such stinginess,
being stingy, state of being stingy, secrecy, meanness, harshness, and the state of a mind that is ungrasping—
this is called stinginess (*macchariya*).

Moreover, stinginess regarding the aggregates (*khandha*) is stinginess; stinginess regarding the elements (*dhātu*) is stinginess; stinginess regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*) is stinginess—this is called stinginess.

One for whom this stinginess has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising again and consumed by the fire of knowledge—that person is called "one who is not stingy."
Free from envy, free from stinginess, modest, and not loathsome.
As for recklessness, there are three kinds of recklessness: [the recklessness of body, speech, and mind].
Bodily insolence, verbal insolence, and mental insolence.
What is bodily insolence?
Herein, someone displays bodily insolence even when in the midst of the Saṅgha, and displays bodily insolence even when in the midst of a group.
He displays physical immodesty in the dining hall; he displays physical immodesty in the sauna;
he displays physical immodesty at the bathing ford; he displays physical immodesty even when entering between houses;
and he displays physical immodesty even once he has entered between houses.
How does one display physical impudence when gone into the Saṅgha?
Here, a certain person, being disrespectful, stands jostling the elder bhikkhus;
he sits jostling them; he stands in front of them; he sits in front of them; he sits on a high seat; and even with his head covered.
He sits down; he speaks while standing; he speaks while waving his arms about.
In this way, he displays physical impudence when among the Saṅgha.
How does he display physical impudence when among a group?
In this case, someone who has joined a group behaves disrespectfully toward elder monks: while they are walking up and down without sandals, he walks up and down wearing sandals;
while they are walking up and down on a low walkway, he walks up and down on a high walkway; while they are walking up and down on the bare ground, he walks up and down on a paved walkway;
he stands in such a way as to brush against them, he sits in such a way as to brush against them, and he stands directly in front of them.
He sits in front [of the teacher], he sits on a high seat, he sits with his head covered;
he speaks while standing, and he speaks while waving his arms about.
In this way, when in a group, he displays physical insolence.
How does one display physical impudence in the dining hall?
Here, someone, out of a lack of respect, sits encroaching upon the elder bhikkhus;
he even obstructs the junior bhikkhus from their seats; he stands jostling them, and he sits jostling them, even in front of them.
He stands [while others are seated], he sits even in front [of others], he sits on a high seat, and he even sits with his head covered;
he speaks while standing, and he speaks while waving his arms.
In this way, he displays physical impudence in the dining hall.
How does one display physical impudence in a sauna?
Here, someone, out of a lack of respect, stands pushing elder bhikkhus in the sauna,
sits pushing them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, and does so without asking permission.
Even without being asked, he throws wood [into the fire], closes the door, and speaks with a swinging of his arms.
In this way, he displays physical impudence in the sauna.
How does he display physical impudence at a bathing place?
In this case, someone might enter a bathing place with a lack of respect for elder bhikkhus, pushing them as he enters, or entering ahead of them;
he bathes while pushing them or bathing ahead of them; he bathes above them;
and he emerges while pushing them or emerging ahead of them or above them.
In this way, he demonstrates physical immodesty at a water-crossing.
How does one entering between houses demonstrate physical immodesty?

Here, a certain person, when entering between houses, out of a lack of respect, passes by jostling elder bhikkhus, or goes ahead of them, or even bypasses the elder bhikkhus and goes right in front of them.
Thus, one entering among the houses displays physical immodesty.
How does one who has entered among the houses display physical immodesty?
Here, a certain person, having entered among the houses, enters even when told, "Do not enter, venerable sir," or "Do not stand."
When told, "Venerable sir, stand," he stands; when told, "Venerable sir, do not sit," he sits;

he enters even where there is no designated place, he stands even where there is no designated place, and he sits even where there is no designated place—even in those private, secluded, and hidden chambers of families.
Wherever noble women, noble daughters, noble daughters-in-law, or noble maidens sit, he enters there impulsively and even touches the head of a young boy.
Thus, having entered among the houses, he displays physical immodesty—
this is what is meant by displaying physical immodesty.

What is verbal insolence? Here, someone displays verbal insolence even when in the midst of the Saṅgha, displays verbal insolence even when in the midst of a group, and displays verbal insolence even when entered among the houses of others.
How does one display verbal insolence when in the midst of the Saṅgha?

In this case, someone who has entered the Saṅgha, acting without due respect, speaks the Dhamma, answers questions, or recites the Pātimokkha to monks who have come to the monastery— either without having asked or consulted the elder bhikkhus;
he speaks while standing, or even while waving his arms about.
In this way, one displays verbal insolence when in the Saṅgha.
How does one display verbal insolence when in a group?

Here, a certain person, having entered a group, without regard for others, and without having asked permission or been requested, speaks Dhamma or answers questions to the monks who have come to the monastery; he speaks while standing, or even while waving his arms about.
When he teaches the Dhamma to bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen who have gone to the monastery, he answers questions; he speaks while standing, or he speaks while waving his arms about.
In this way, one displays verbal impudence when in a group.
How does one display verbal impudence when entered among the houses?
In this case, someone who has entered among the houses says to a woman or a girl:
"Lady so-and-so of such-and-such a clan, what is there?
Is there rice-gruel? Is there cooked rice? Is there solid food?"
"What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we chew?
What is there? Or what will you give me?"—to prattle thus, which is such speech as idle chatter, prattling, lamenting, the state of lamenting, the act of lamenting.
In this way, having entered among the houses, one displays verbal insolence.
This is verbal insolence.
What is mental insolence?
Here, someone who has gone forth from a high family does not regard himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a high family.
He esteems himself by way of his mind; being one who has gone forth from a great family, he does not esteem himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a great family;
being one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth, he does not esteem himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth;
being one who has gone forth from a family of abundant wealth... nor as a master of the Suttantas.
Being a master of the Suttantas, he considers himself equal to them in mind;
yet he is not [truly] a master of the Vinaya... not a preacher of the Dhamma... not a forest-dweller... not an alms-food eater...
not a wearer of rag-robes... not a wearer of the three robes... not one who goes on uninterrupted alms-round... not one who eats only from the single bowl.
Being one who practices in a sitting posture... being one who does not practice in a sitting posture... being one who does not accept any seat as it is offered...
being one who has not attained the first jhāna, he does not regard himself as equal in mind to one who has attained the first jhāna...

[and so on] ...being one who has not attained the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he does not regard himself as equal in mind to one who has attained the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is mental insolence (*pāgabbhiya*).

One for whom these three forms of insolence have been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one who is not insolent" (*appagabbha*). Thus, he is "one who is not insolent."
"Disgusting.
There is a person who is disgusting, and there is one who is not disgusting.
And what kind of person is disgusting?

Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, impure and suspicious in his conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be one, not living the holy life though claiming to do so, inwardly rotten, leaking, and corrupt—this is called the person who is loathsome.
Or else, he is prone to anger and full of vexation; even when spoken to only slightly, he becomes resentful, agitated, malicious, and stubborn, manifesting anger, hatred, and resentment.
This person is called loathsome.
Alternatively, he is prone to anger and resentment; he is slanderous and spiteful; he is envious and stingy; he is fraudulent and deceitful; he is stubborn and excessively conceited;
he has evil desires and wrong view; and he is one who clings to his own immediate opinions as supreme.
One who grasps at what is taken up and is difficult to let go of—
this person is called repulsive.
And what kind of person is non-repulsive?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training—this person is called one who is not loathsome.

Or else, he is free from anger and does not harbor much resentment; even when spoken to at length, he does not become vexed, does not become agitated, does not fall into ill will, does not remain obstinate, and does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
This person is called one who is not loathsome.
Alternatively, he is without anger and without malice; he is without hypocrisy and without spite;

he is without envy and without avarice; he is without deceit and without guile; he is without stubbornness and without arrogance; he does not have evil desires nor wrong view, and he does not cling to his own opinions.
One who does not grasp with attachment and is easy to relinquish—this person is called "one who is not disgusted.
All foolish worldlings are disgusted; from the "virtuous worldling" upward, the eight noble persons are "not disgusted."
"Free from arrogance and free from disgust;
not intent on slander. Regarding "slander":

here, someone is a speaker of divisive speech; having heard something here, he reports it there for the sake of dividing these people, or having heard something there, he reports it here for the sake of dividing those people.

Thus, one who breaks those who are united, or incites others to break those who are divided; one who delights in factions, rejoices in factions, finds pleasure in factions, and utters speech that causes division—this is called malicious talebearing (*pesuñña*).
Furthermore, one instigates malicious talebearing for two reasons:
Either out of a desire for affection or with the intention to cause division.
How does one engage in slander out of a desire for affection?
Thinking: "I shall become dear to him, I shall become pleasing to him, I shall become trustworthy, I shall become intimate, I shall become well-disposed toward him."
Thus one engages in malicious speech out of a desire for affection.
How does one engage in malicious speech with the intention of causing division?

[One thinks: "How might these people become divided, separated, factionalized, split, alienated, and split into two parties; how might they break apart and not come together, so that they dwell in suffering and lack comfort?"
Thus one engages in slander with the intention of causing division.

But he for whom this slander has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, who is incapable of its recurrence, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—he is not addicted to slander, not engaged in it, not devoted to it, and not rightly intent upon it;
thus he is not addicted to malicious speech.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Withdrawn, free from guile,
without envy and without stinginess;”
“Free from immodesty, free from disgust,
and not addicted to slander; one who does not pursue worldly pleasures.”
He is not intent on conceit;
he is gentle and eloquent,
yet neither faithful nor dispassionate.
"Unheeding among the alluring things.
By "alluring things" (sātiya) are meant the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañca kāmaguṇā).
For what reason are the five strands of sensual pleasure called "alluring things"?
For the most part, gods and humans desire, relish, long for, crave, and yearn for the five strands of sensual pleasure; for that reason, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called "relishing.
For those in whom this craving as relishing has not been abandoned, craving for forms flows, leaks out, streams forth, and proceeds from the eye;
craving for sounds from the ear... craving for odors from the nose... craving for flavors from the tongue... craving for tangibles from the body.
... from the mind, craving for phenomena flows out, flows forth, streams out, and proceeds.

For those in whom this craving has been abandoned through this mindfulness, severed, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—for them, craving for forms does not flow out from the eye, does not flow forth, does not stream out, and does not proceed.
Craving for sounds from the ear …pe… craving for mental phenomena from the mind does not flow out, does not flow forth, does not stream out, and does not proceed— thus,
one is "one who does not leak" regarding the objects of craving.
"And conceit is not suitable for us.
What is conceit?
Here, someone treats another with contempt on account of birth, or clan, or... [as before] ...or on account of some other basis.

Whatever kind of conceit there is—conceiving, the state of conceiving, loftiness, haughtiness, a banner, grasping, the desire for self-display in the mind—this is called overweening conceit (*atimāna*).

One for whom this overweening conceit has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge—that person is not engaged in overweening conceit; he is not engaged, not improperly engaged, and is rightly engaged.
And he is not intent on conceit.
He is gentle and eloquent. "Gentle" means:
he is endowed with gentle bodily action; he is gentle through gentle verbal action; [he is gentle] through gentle mental action.
“Endowed” means gentle. One who is endowed with the gentle foundations of mindfulness is gentle;
one who is endowed with the gentle right efforts … the gentle bases of psychic power … the gentle faculties … the gentle powers … the gentle factors of enlightenment is gentle;
one who is endowed with the gentle Noble Eightfold Path is gentle.
Gentle.
"Eloquent" refers to three kinds of eloquence:
eloquence regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti*), eloquence regarding inquiry (*paripucchā*), and eloquence regarding realization (*adhigama*).
What is one who possesses inspired eloquence through mastery of the scriptures? Here, someone has by nature mastered the scriptures—

the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and question-and-answer texts— and relying upon that mastery, he speaks with inspired eloquence.
This is one who possesses inspired eloquence regarding the scriptures.

What is one who possesses inspired eloquence through inquiry? Here, someone is an inquirer regarding his own welfare, the meaning of knowledge, characteristics, reasons, and what is possible and impossible; and based on that inquiry, he becomes inspired.
This one possesses eloquence regarding inquiry.
Who possesses eloquence regarding realization?
Here, someone has realized the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases for psychic power.
The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the four noble paths,
the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges, and the six direct knowledges—
his meaning is known, his doctrine is known, and his terminology is known.
When the meaning is known, the meaning becomes manifest;
when the Dharma is known, the Dharma becomes manifest;
when the language is known, the language becomes manifest.
Among these three types of knowledge, knowledge is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
One who is endowed with this analytical knowledge of perspicuity—fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, fully attained, and possessed of it—is called "eloquent" (*paṭibhānavā*).
For one who lacks mastery of the scriptures, lacks thorough inquiry, and lacks realization, what will there be for him to be eloquent about?
"Gentle and eloquent.
'Neither faithful nor dispassionate'—

as for 'not faithful,' he does not place faith in anyone else— whether another ascetic or brahmin, or a deva, Māra, or Brahmā— in a Dhamma that has been personally realized through direct higher knowledge by himself."
“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’—this has been directly known by me through my own higher knowledge...
‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering’...
‘All phenomena are non-self’...”
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise” …pe… “With birth as condition,
aging-and-death arise” … “With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease” …pe…
“With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death”… “This is suffering”… [and so on] “… this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
“These are the taints” …pe… “this is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints” … “these phenomena are to be directly known” …pe…
“‘These phenomena are to be realized’—this has been directly known by himself through his own higher knowledge...

[and so on] ...the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape regarding the six bases of contact; the arising... [and so on] ...the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging;
and the arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape regarding the four great elements—all this has been directly known by himself through his own higher knowledge... [and so on]...”
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation”— this Dhamma he has personally realized through direct higher knowledge for himself,
and he does not rely on the faith of anyone else, whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Do you have faith, Sāriputta, that the faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and culminates in the Deathless?
The faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness …”
“Is the faculty of concentration … the faculty of wisdom developed and cultivated so that it plunges into the Deathless, tends toward the Deathless, and culminates in the Deathless?
“I do not go by faith in the Blessed One in this matter, venerable sir, regarding the faculty of faith …”
the faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness … the faculty of concentration …
The faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its final goal, and culminates in the Deathless.

For those, venerable sir, who have not known this, have not seen it, have not understood it, have not realized it, and have not touched it with wisdom, they would proceed therein by faith in others, [thinking]:
"The faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless..."
It has the deathless as its destination, the deathless as its consummation.
The faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness … [likewise].
The faculty of concentration… the faculty of wisdom,
when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and culminates in the Deathless.
But those, venerable sir, by whom this is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom— they are there free from doubt and devoid of uncertainty.
The faculty of faith … the faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness …
The faculty of concentration… the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its final goal, and culminates in the Deathless.
And this, venerable sir, is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by me through wisdom; I am without doubt and free from uncertainty regarding it.
The faculty of faith … the faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness …
“The faculty of concentration… the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, has the deathless as its ground, the deathless as its destination, and the deathless as its consummation.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”

“Sāriputta, those for whom this is unknown, unseen, unrecognized, unverified, and not touched by wisdom would have to proceed therein on the basis of faith in others. [For them] the faculty of faith... up to ...
the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, becomes immersed in the Deathless, has the Deathless as its goal, and culminates in the Deathless.
One who lacks faith and is ungrateful... [is lost].
The man who has severed the connection,
whose opportunity is destroyed and whose hope is vomited out—
he indeed is the supreme person.
"He neither has faith nor is dispassionate":
all foolish worldlings are passionate; starting from the "good worldling," the seven types of trainees are dispassionate.

The Arahant neither is passionate nor is dispassionate; he is dispassionate because of the destruction of lust through being free from lust, because of the destruction of hatred through being free from hatred, and because of the destruction of delusion through being free from delusion.

Thus, having completed his residence [in the training] and practiced the conduct... [pe] ...there is no further becoming for him in the saṃsāra of birth and death—thus, one who lacks faith does not become dispassionate.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
One who does not fail to listen to the wise, who is not devoted to arrogance,
who is gentle and eloquent—
“He is neither faithful nor dispassionate.
Desiring gain, he does not train;
and when there is no gain, he becomes angry.
He is not at odds with craving,
nor does he greedily hanker after flavors.
He does not train out of a desire for gain, nor does he become angry when there is no gain.
How does one train out of a desire for gain?
Here, monks, a monk sees another monk who is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
It occurs to him:
“By what means does this venerable one obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?
It occurs to him:
“This venerable one is a master of the discourses; that is why this venerable one obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
Thus, for the sake of gain, with gain as condition, with gain as cause, for the production of gain, while seeking to bring gain to fruition, he masters the discourses.
In this way, too, he trains out of desire for gain.
Or else, a bhikkhu sees another bhikkhu who is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
It occurs to him:
"By what means has this venerable one become a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?
It occurs to him thus:
“This venerable one is indeed a master of the Vinaya … a preacher of the Dhamma … a master of the Abhidhamma;
it is because of this that this venerable one receives robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
Thus, for the sake of gain, with gain as condition, with gain as cause, and for the production of gain, one who is maturing gain masters the Abhidhamma.
In this way too, one trains out of desire for gain.
Or else, a bhikkhu sees another bhikkhu who is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The thought occurs to him:
"By what means has this venerable one become a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?
The thought occurs to him thus:
“This venerable one is indeed a forest-dweller… an alms-food eater… a wearer of rag-robes….”
One who wears only three robes… one who goes for alms in regular order… one who eats only from a single alms-bowl after the midday meal…
“He is one who never sits down...
he is one who accepts whatever seat is assigned; therefore this venerable one is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
For the sake of gain, with gain as his motive, through the cause of gain, and for the production of gain, he becomes a forest-dweller while seeking to mature that gain... [and so on].
He is one who uses whatever seat is provided.
In this way, too, he trains out of a desire for gain.
How does he train without a desire for gain?
Here, a bhikkhu does not, for the sake of gain, nor with gain as a condition, nor for the cause of gain,

nor for the production of gain, nor while seeking to bring gain to maturity, master the Suttantas, master the Vinaya, or master the Abhidhamma; rather, he masters them solely for the purpose of self-taming, for the purpose of self-mastery, and for the purpose of self-parinibbāna.
In this way, too, he trains not out of desire for gain.
Or rather, a bhikkhu does not, for the sake of gain, nor with gain as cause, nor with gain as motive, nor for the production of gain,
nor while maturing gain, train in anything other than being based on fewness of wishes, based on contentment, and based on effacement.
Relying solely on seclusion, relying solely on this very purpose, he becomes a forest-dweller, an alms-food eater, a wearer of rag-robes,
a wearer of the three robes, one who goes for alms in regular order, one who eats only from a single bowl, a sitter,
and one who accepts whatever seat is offered.
Thus, "one does not train out of desire for gain" means one does not train out of desire for gain;
and "one is not disturbed by lack of gain."
How does one become angry when there is no gain?

Here, someone thinks: "I do not obtain a family, or I do not obtain a group, or I do not obtain a dwelling, or I do not obtain gain, or I do not obtain fame, or I do not obtain praise, or I do not obtain happiness."
If he does not obtain robes, or does not obtain almsfood, or does not obtain lodgings, or does not obtain medicinal requisites for the sick,
or does not obtain an attendant for the sick, he thinks, "I am unknown," and he becomes angry, becomes resentful, becomes stubborn,
and manifests anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction.
Thus one is disturbed by lack of gain.
How is one not disturbed by lack of gain?
Here, a bhikkhu thinks: "I do not obtain a family, or I do not obtain a group... [and so on].
Thinking, "I am not renowned," he does not become angry, does not become ill-tempered, does not become stubborn, and he does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
Thus, he does not become angry when there is no gain; thus, one who desires gain does not train [in this way], yet he does not become angry when there is no gain.
"And unopposed by craving, he does not greedily hanker after flavors. "Opposed" means:

that which is an irritation of the mind, an aversion, hostility, opposition, anger, provocation, intense provocation, hatred, malice, intense malice, a corruption of the mind, mental corruption, wrath, being wrathful, the state of being wrathful.
Hatred, being hateful, the state of being hateful; malice, being malicious, the state of being malicious;
opposition, counter-opposition, ferocity, abruptness, and mental dissatisfactoriness—this is called opposition.
He for whom this opposition has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one who is not opposed.
"Craving" (*taṇhā*) refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.

"Taste" (*rasa*) refers to the taste of roots, the taste of trunks, the taste of bark, the taste of leaves, the taste of flowers, and the taste of fruits; it includes sour, sweet, bitter, pungent, salty, alkaline, astringent, and acrid flavors; and it includes what is savory and insipid, cold and hot.
Some ascetics and brahmins are greedy for flavors.
Seeking the finest flavors with the tip of their tongues, they wander about; having obtained something sour, they seek what is not sour; having obtained what is not sour, they seek what is sour;
having obtained something sweet, they seek what is not sweet; having obtained what is not sweet, they seek what is sweet.
Having obtained something bitter, they seek what is not bitter; having obtained what is not bitter, they seek what is bitter.
Having obtained something pungent, they seek what is not pungent; having obtained what is not pungent, they seek what is pungent.
Having obtained something salty, they seek what is not salty; having obtained what is not salty, they seek what is salty.
Having obtained something savory, they seek out what is unsavory; having obtained what is unsavory, they seek out what is savory.
Having obtained something sweet, they seek out what is bitter; having obtained what is bitter, they seek out what is sweet.
Having obtained something delicious, they seek out what is undelicious; having obtained what is undelicious, they seek out what is delicious.
Having obtained cold, they seek heat; having obtained heat, they seek cold.

Whatever they obtain, they are not satisfied with that, but seek more and more. They are attached to, greedy for, infatuated with, muddled by, obsessed with, stuck to, clung to, and fettered by agreeable tastes.

But one for whom this craving for tastes has been abandoned, utterly destroyed, stilled, and subsided—rendered incapable of arising and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—that person consumes food with wise reflection.

Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification, but only for the endurance and maintenance of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Thus, I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, so that there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
Just as one might sprinkle a forest with water only for the purpose of planting, or just as one might oil a cart-axle only for the purpose of [its smooth operation]...
Just as one might consume the flesh of one's own son as food solely for the purpose of crossing a desert, so too does a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, consume food:
"not for amusement... [but] for the maintenance of this body and for its comfort."

He abandons craving for tastes, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. He is one who is detached from craving for tastes, abstinent, refrained from it, emerged from it, escaped from it, and liberated; he dwells with a mind that has transcended its boundaries.
Thus, being unopposed by craving, he does not lust after tastes.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
One who does not train out of desire for gain,
who is not disturbed by lack of gain,
and who is free from conflict with craving—
“He does not crave after flavors.
Always equanimous and mindful,
he does not conceive of anything as equal in the world.
Neither superior nor inferior,
he has no mental excitements;
he is always equanimous and mindful.
"Equanimous" means he is endowed with the sixfold equanimity:
having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

Having seen a pleasing form with the eye, one does not crave it, does not lust after it, and does not generate passion for it; his body remains steadfast, and his mind is internally steady, well-composed, and well-liberated.

But when one has seen a disagreeable form with the eye, one does not become dejected; one remains with a mind that is unestablished, a heart that is undepressed, and a consciousness that is uncorrupted. His body remains steady, and his mind is internally stable, well-composed, and well-liberated.
When one has heard a sound with the ear...
when one has smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not crave it, does not lust after it, and does not generate passion toward it. His body remains steady; his mind remains steady, well-composed within, and well-liberated.

But having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not dejected by what is disagreeable; his mind is unshaken, his mental state is undepressed, and his heart is free from ill will. His body remains steady, and his mind is steady, well-composed within, and well-liberated.
Having seen a form with the eye, regarding forms that are agreeable or disagreeable, his body remains steady, and his mind is steady, well-composed within, and well-liberated.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, his body remains steady amidst phenomena that are agreeable and disagreeable; his mind remains steady within, well-composed and well-liberated.

Having seen a form with the eye, he is not excited by what is provocative of lust, not repelled by what is provocative of aversion, not deluded by what is provocative of delusion, not agitated by what is provocative of anger, not intoxicated by what is provocative of pride, and not defiled by what is provocative of the defilements.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].

Having cognized a phenomenon with the mind, one does not become lustful toward what is lust-inducing, does not become hateful toward what is hate-inducing, does not become deluded by what is delusion-inducing, does not become angry at what is anger-inducing, does not become intoxicated by what is intoxication-inducing, and does not become defiled by what is defilement-inducing.
One is merely a seer of the seen, a hearer of the heard, a feeler of the felt, and a cognizer of the cognized.
One is not smeared by the seen, not smeared by the heard, not smeared by the felt, and not smeared by the cognized.

One dwells with a mind that is unattached to what is seen, undepressed, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated— free from the boundaries of the measurable. [The same applies to] what is heard … what is sensed … what is cognized … [one dwells with a mind that is unattached, undepressed, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated— free from the boundaries of the measurable].
Regarding what is cognized, he dwells unattached, undistressed, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind for which no limits exist.
The eye exists for the Arahant; the Arahant sees forms with the eye.
Yet lustful desire does not exist for the Arahant; the Arahant is one whose mind is well-liberated.
The ear exists for the Arahant; the Arahant hears sound with the ear.
There is no lustful desire in the Arahant; the Arahant is well-liberated in mind.
The nose exists for the Arahant; the Arahant smells odor with the nose.
Lustful passion does not exist in the Arahant; the Arahant is one whose mind is well-liberated.
The tongue exists for the Arahant; the Arahant tastes flavor with the tongue...
[as before] ...the body exists for the Arahant; the Arahant touches the tangible with the body... [as before].
The mind of an arahant exists; the arahant cognizes mental phenomena with the mind.
An arahant has no desire or lust; the arahant is well-liberated in mind.
The eye delights in forms, takes pleasure in forms, and rejoices in forms; that [eye] of the arahant is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.
The ear delights in sounds...
the nose delights in odors...
the tongue delights in tastes, is fond of tastes, and rejoices in tastes; yet for the Arahant, it is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.
The body delights in tactile objects...

[and so on] ...the mind delights in mental phenomena, rejoices in mental phenomena, and exults in mental phenomena. That [body, etc. of the Arahant is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained; and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint:
"They lead the tamed one to the assembly..."
The tamed one the king mounts;
the tamed one is the best among humans,
who endures abuse.
Better than mules,
and even than noble Sindh horses,
are the great elephants, the mighty tuskers.
One who has tamed oneself is better than those.
For by means of these vehicles,
one could not go to the destination that has not yet been reached.
Just as one who is tamed goes with a well-tamed self,
they do not waver amidst various circumstances.
Completely liberated from renewed existence,
having reached the stage of the tamed,
they are victors in the world.
He whose faculties are cultivated both internally and externally throughout the entire world,
having become disillusioned with this world and the world beyond—
“He awaits his time, developed and self-controlled.
“Ever equanimous”:
ever means at all times, at every moment, constantly, perpetually... [etc.]
In the final stage of life.
"Mindful" means mindful for four reasons:
being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness that consists in the contemplation of the body as a body.
Developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating feelings … the mind … phenomena as phenomena, he dwells mindful … [and so on].
Thus he is called "mindful"—
equanimous and always mindful.
He does not conceive of anything in the world as "equal."
“He does not generate the conceit ‘I am equal’ on account of birth, or clan, or any other such basis;
thus he does not conceive of himself as equal in the world.
He does not conceive of himself as superior, nor as inferior.”
“He is superior to me”—thus he does not give rise to overweening pride on account of birth, clan, or any other such basis.
“I am inferior to him”—thus he does not give rise to self-depreciation on account of birth, clan, or any other such basis.
Thus he is neither conceited nor lowly.
"He has no excesses.
"His" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Excesses" refers to the seven excesses (sattussada).
The excess of lust, the excess of hatred, the excess of delusion, the excess of conceit, the excess of views, the excess of defilements, and the excess of kamma.

These excesses do not exist in him; they do not exist, are not found, and are not apprehended. They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided; they are incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Thus, "for him there are no excesses."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Ever equanimous and mindful,
one does not conceive of anything as equal in the world.”
“He is neither superior nor inferior;
for him there are no haughtinesses. For one who has no dependence—
Having understood the Dhamma and being independent,
for whom there exists no craving for either existence or non-existence.
"Of whom there is no dependence.
"Of whom" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Dependence" refers to two kinds of dependence: [dependence on requisites and dependence on a teacher].
The dependence on craving and the dependence on views ... [as before] ...
this is dependence on craving ... [as before] ... this is dependence on views.
