For him, the dependence on craving has been abandoned and the dependence on views has been relinquished.
Because dependence on craving has been abandoned and dependence on views has been relinquished, that state of dependence— which does not exist,
is not present, is not found, and is not obtained— is abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
There is no dependence for him.
"Having known the Dhamma as independent":

"having known" means having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified; having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, fully clarified, and made manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."

“Having known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering’ … ‘all phenomena are non-self’ … and ‘whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation,’ [he does so] by making it manifest.”
"Independent": there are two dependencies—the dependency of craving and the dependency of views... [as follows] ...this is the dependency of craving... [as follows] ...
This is reliance on views.

Having abandoned reliance on craving and relinquished reliance on views, one is not dependent on the eye, not dependent on the ear, not dependent on the nose, not dependent on the tongue, not dependent on the body, not dependent on the mind, [not dependent on] forms … sounds … [smells … tastes … tactile objects … mental phenomena].
In odors … in tastes … in tangibles …
A family … a group … a residence … [and so forth] …

"Knowing the Dhamma as one who is independent"—this refers to one who dwells with a mind that is independent, unattached, not drawn toward, not clung to, and not obsessed regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; who has gone out from them, escaped them, is liberated from them, and is dissociated from them, dwelling with a mind free from boundaries.
"In whom no craving for existence or non-existence exists."
"Craving" means craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
"Of whom" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"For existence" means for the view of eternalism; "for non-existence" means for the view of annihilationism.
"For existence" means for the sake of the eternalist view; "for non-existence" means for the sake of the annihilationist view.
"For existence" means for the sake of repeated becoming, repeated destinies, repeated births, repeated rebirths, and repeated production of individuality.

One in whom craving does not exist, does not persist, is not found, and is not perceived—one by whom it has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—[for such a one, there is no future existence].
For one in whom craving for existence or non-existence does not exist—
therefore the Blessed One said:
“He for whom there is no dependence...”
Having understood the Dhamma and being independent,
for whom there exists no craving either for existence or for non-existence.
I call him "peaceful," who has no longing for sensual pleasures; for him,
the fetters do not exist.
He has crossed over attachment.
That person I call "peaceful"—
one who is stilled, calmed, extinguished, and tranquilized.
"I say that, I speak that, I declare that, I illuminate that, I express that—
I say that he is 'peaceful.
He is one who has no longing for sensual pleasures."
Regarding "sensual pleasures" (*kāma*): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasure—sensual pleasure as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure as defilements (*kilesakāma*).
… [omission] … these are called sensual pleasure as objects. … [omission] …
These are called the defilement-desires. Having fully understood the object-desires, and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the defilement-desires,
one is without regard for sensual pleasures— one who is free from desire, who has cast off desire, vomited out desire, released desire, abandoned desire, and renounced desire.
"One who is free from passion for sensual pleasures, devoid of passion, with passion abandoned, cast off, released, and relinquished; one who is hungerless,
extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, and dwells having become Brahmā himself"—
this refers to one who has no regard for sensual pleasures.
"His fetters do not exist.
Fetters are the four fetters:
the bodily fetter of covetousness, the bodily fetter of ill will, the bodily fetter of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily fetter of dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth."
Lust for one’s own view is the bodily tie of covetousness; resentment toward the doctrines of others is the bodily tie of ill will;
misapprehension of one’s own virtue, observance, or both virtue and observance is the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances;
and the insistence that “only this is the truth” regarding one’s own view is the bodily tie of dogmatic belief in a doctrine.
"Of him" means of the arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"No knots exist for him": for him there are no knots;
they do not exist, they are not found, they are not obtained. They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided; they are incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
No knots exist for him;
he has crossed over attachment.
"Attachment" is said to be craving.
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
In what sense is it "clinging" (*visattikā*)?
It is clinging because it is "stuck" (*visatā*).
The craving that is extensive,
the craving that has spread out,
the craving that is uneven.
It clings, thus it is clinging;
it spreads, thus it is clinging;
it deceives, thus it is clinging.
Craving is like poisonous roots;
craving is like poisonous fruits;
craving is like the enjoyment of poison.

Or rather, that craving (*taṇhā*) is called "clinging" (*visattikā*) because it is spread out and extended over forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clans, groups, dwellings, and so forth, up to all phenomena seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
"He has crossed over clinging":
he has crossed, traversed, surmounted, and transcended this clinging, which is craving.
He has crossed over the attachment to existence.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"I call him one who is stilled."
For one who has no longing for sensual pleasures,
the fetters do not exist;
he has crossed over attachment.
For him there are no sons,
no livestock, no fields, and no land;
neither self nor what belongs to a self exists.
"In that [self], nothing is found;
neither sons nor cattle, nor field nor property exists.
This "not" is a negation (*paṭikkhepa*).
"Of him" means of the arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Sons" refers to four kinds of sons:
a son born of oneself, a son born of the field, a son given away, and a pupil as a son.
"Livestock" means goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mules.
"Field" means a field of rice, a field of paddy, a field of green gram, a field of black gram, a field of barley, a field of wheat, or a field of sesame.
"Property" means the site of a house, the site of a storehouse, the site of a city, the site of a village, the site of a park, or the site of a monastery.
"He has no sons, nor cattle, nor field, nor property" means that he has no possession of sons,
no possession of cattle, no possession of fields, and no possession of property.
They do not exist, they are not found, they are not apprehended; they have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided;
incapable of arising again, they are burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus, for him, there are no children or cattle, nor does field or land exist.
"Neither self nor non-self is found therein.
"Self" refers to the view of a self (*attadiṭṭhi*); "non-self" refers to the view of annihilation (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).
There is nothing grasped as "self," and there is nothing to be relinquished as "non-self."
For one who has nothing grasped, there is nothing to be released.
For one who has nothing to be released, there is nothing grasped.
Having transcended grasping and releasing, the Arahant has gone beyond increase and decrease.
Thus, having completed his residence and practiced the course of conduct... [as before] ...for him there is no more wandering in birth and death, no further becoming;
neither a self nor a non-self is found in him.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For him there are no children or livestock,
nor does he possess fields or land;
neither self nor what belongs to a self exists.”
“Is not found therein.
That by which ordinary people,
as well as ascetics and brahmins, might describe him—
That is not held before him;
therefore, he is not led astray by doctrines—
whether those by which worldly people would describe him, or as "ascetics" and "brahmins."

“Ordinary persons” (*puthujjana*): they are called ordinary persons because they generate various defilements; they are called ordinary persons because they have not abandoned the various views of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);
they are called ordinary persons because they look toward the faces of various teachers; they are called ordinary persons because they have not emerged from the various realms of existence;
they are called ordinary persons because they perform various diverse volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*); they are called ordinary persons because they are swept away by various floods (*ogha*).
They are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various individual fevers; they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various individual anxieties;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually attached, greedy, infatuated, maddened, obsessed, clinging, stuck, and entangled in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually shrouded, covered, enveloped, and obstructed by the five hindrances.
"Concealed and covered up" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"Ascetics" (*samaṇa*) refers to anyone who has gone forth externally from here and has entered the life of a wanderer.
"Brahmins" refers to those who address others with "bho" (sir).
As for what ordinary people might call him— namely, "ascetics and brahmins"—
it is by whatever passion, hatred, or delusion ordinary people might speak of him.
Whatever conceit they might speak with, whatever view they might speak with, whatever restlessness they might speak with,
whatever doubt they might speak with, or whatever underlying tendencies they might speak with—
whether as "lustful," "hateful," "deluded," "bound," "adherent," "distracted," "gone astray," or "established"— those volitional formations have been abandoned.
Because of the abandoning of volitional formations, there is no ground by which they might say of him:

"He is a denizen of hell," or "He is one of the animal realm," or "He is in the sphere of hungry ghosts," or "He is a human," or "He is a deva," or "He is possessed of form," or "He is formless," or "He is percipient," or "He is non-percipient," or "He is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
There is no cause, no condition, and no reason by which they might say of him, speak of him, declare him, describe him, or designate him thus.
"That by which ordinary people, as well as recluses and brahmins,
might speak of him— that is not held before him.
"Of him" refers to the arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Preoccupation": there are two kinds of preoccupation—the preoccupation with craving and the preoccupation with views... [as before] ...this is the preoccupation with craving... [as before] ...
This is one who prioritizes views.
For him, the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished.
Because the prioritizing of craving has been abandoned and the prioritizing of views has been relinquished, he does not [cling] to craving or to views.
Or, having placed [something] in front, he walks; he does not have craving as his banner, craving as his standard, or craving as his overlord;
he does not have views as his banner, views as his standard, or views as his overlord; he does not walk surrounded by either craving or views—this is what is "not placed in front" for him.
"Therefore, he does not waver in the face of disputes.

"Therefore" means for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, by that source; because of disputes, accusations, censures, reproaches, dispraise, and defamation, he does not waver, does not shake, does not move, does not tremble, does not quiver, does not quake—he does not waver in the face of disputes.
Therefore, he does not waver in the face of disputes.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“That by which ordinary people, as well as recluses and brahmins, might speak of him...”
That is not held before him;
therefore he is not led astray by disputes.
Free from greed and without envy...
The Sage does not speak in praise of the superior,
nor of the equal, nor of the inferior; being himself beyond conventional status,
he leads others toward that which is beyond status.
"Free from greed and without envy.
Greed is said to be craving—that which is lust, infatuation, ... down to ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
He whose greed has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed; which is incapable of arising again and has been burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called one who is free from greed.
He is not greedy for forms...

[and so on] ...he is not greedy, not infatuated, not deluded, and not clinging to things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Free from greed, devoid of greed, having cast off greed, having left greed behind, released from greed, having abandoned greed, having relinquished greed, he is free from hunger... [and so on].
"He dwells with himself become Brahmā" means he is free from lust.
"He is not miserly": as for miserliness, there are five kinds of miserliness.
Stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding praise, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.
Whatever is such as this... [and so on] ...grasping.
This is called stinginess (*macchariya*).

One for whom this stinginess has been abandoned, utterly destroyed, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and consumed by the fire of knowledge— that one is called "free from stinginess" (*amaccharī*)—
one who is devoid of greed and free from stinginess.
The sage does not speak in praise of superiors, nor of equals, nor of inferiors—thus it is said, "the sage.
"Sage" (muni): "Mona" is called knowledge... [and so on] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
“He says ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—he does not say, speak, utter, illuminate, or declare such things.
Thus the sage does not speak of superiors, nor of equals, nor of inferiors;
he leads through the aeon as one who is beyond what is unallowable.
“Eras” means two eras:
the era of craving and the era of views … [as before] … this is the era of craving … [as before] …
This is the conceptualization of views.
For him, the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished.

Because the conceptualization of craving has been abandoned and the conceptualization of views has been relinquished, he does not lead away toward, nor approach, nor go toward, nor grasp, nor misapprehend, nor adhere to either the conceptualization of craving or the conceptualization of views.
He carries it for a kappa.
"Unallowable" means:
there are two kinds of allowable things—
The conceptualization of craving and the conceptualization of views...
[as before] ...this is the conceptualization of craving... [as before] ...this is the conceptualization of views.
His construction of craving has been abandoned, his construction of views has been relinquished.

Because the construction of craving has been abandoned and the construction of views has been relinquished, he does not construct, generate, produce, bring about, or cause to arise either the construction of craving or the construction of views.
Thus, he leads away from construction, being one who is beyond construction.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Free from greed and without envy,
the sage does not speak in praise of those who excel him.”
Neither among equals nor among inferiors does one who is unworthy lead another for an eon.
He for whom there is nothing of his own in the world—
He does not grieve over what is non-existent,
nor does he pursue worldly phenomena;
he indeed is called "the peaceful one."
“He who has nothing of his own in the world.
“He who” refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
“Has nothing of his own in the world” means: [he has no sense of ownership].

For me, there is nothing whatsoever pertaining to form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness—whether my own or that of others—which has been grasped, clung to, adhered to, craved after, or committed to; it does not exist...
[as before] ...it has been burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
"He who has nothing of his own in the world,
and does not grieve over what is non-existent":
he does not grieve over an object that has changed, nor does he grieve when an object has changed.
"My eye has changed"—he does not grieve.
"My ear... "My nose... [he does not grieve.]
My tongue...
my body...
my mind...
Forms are mine… sounds are mine… smells are mine…
Tastes are mine… tangible objects are mine… my family is mine…
The assembly is mine...
my dwelling is mine...
my gain is mine...
My fame...

my happiness...
“Robe-cloth for me… almsfood for me… a resting place for me…”
The requisite of medicine as support for the sick is mine...
my mother is mine...
my father is mine...
My brother...
my sister...
my son...
My daughter...
my friends...
my ministers...
"My kinsmen...
my blood relations have changed"—he does not grieve, he does not weary, he does not lament, he does not beat his breast, he does not fall into confusion.
In this way also, he does not grieve over what is non-existent.

Alternatively, when touched, overcome, afflicted, and possessed by an unpleasant and painful feeling, he does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.

When touched, overcome, afflicted, and possessed by an eye disease, he does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion; [the same applies when] touched by an ear disease...

"Though touched by gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles, though beset, oppressed, afflicted, and overcome by them, he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion.
In this way, too, he does not grieve because of what is non-existent.
Or alternatively, because it is non-existent, not found, and not perceived—

Thinking, “Alas, that I do not have this! Oh, that I might have this! Alas, I do not obtain it! he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion. Thus, he does not grieve over what is non-existent, nor does he go astray among phenomena;
that is to say, he does not go astray through desire, he does not go astray through hatred, and he does not go astray through delusion.
He goes; he does not go by way of fear, he does not go under the influence of lust,
he does not go under the influence of hatred, he does not go under the influence of delusion, he does not go under the influence of conceit, he does not go under the influence of views,
he does not go under the influence of restlessness, he does not go under the influence of doubt, he does not go under the influence of underlying tendencies, nor does he go by way of divisive states.
"He goes, he is led, he is carried away, he is swept along"—
yet he does not go among phenomena.
He is indeed called "the peaceful one."
Thus, being calm, tranquil, stilled, extinguished, and serene, one is said, proclaimed, spoken of, uttered, illustrated,
and designated as "one who is at peace.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“He who has nothing of his own in the world,
who does not grieve over what is non-existent,
and who does not pursue worldly phenomena— ”
“He is indeed called ‘the peaceful.
This concludes the tenth exposition, the Purābheda Sutta.
